analogy.p: Imagine the house's central heating: the **thermostat** (the thermoregulatory centre) senses the room temperature, and when it is too cold it switches the **boiler on and closes the windows** (shivering, vasoconstriction, hairs on end), but when it is too warm it **opens the windows and turns on the fan** (vasodilation and sweating). Once the room is back at the set temperature the thermostat switches the response off, so the temperature wobbles gently around the target. The analogy breaks down because the body has many effectors working at once, it uses nerves and not electrical wires, and the temperature is not just room air but the blood flowing through every organ.

bullets: **Normal body temperature** is about **37 °C**, the temperature at which human **enzymes work best**.
**Thermoregulatory centre**: in the brain; has receptors sensitive to the **temperature of the blood** flowing through it.
**Skin temperature receptors**: send impulses (a nervous message) to the thermoregulatory centre about the temperature at the surface.
**Too hot**: **sweat glands release sweat**, and **blood vessels dilate** (vasodilation).
**Too cold**: **skeletal muscles contract** rapidly (**shivering**), **blood vessels constrict** (vasoconstriction), **hairs stand on end**, and **sweating stops**.
Be able to explain each response using the idea of **energy transfer** to or from the surroundings.
Typical marks: 1 mark for naming a response, 2 to 3 marks for explaining why it works, 4 to 6 marks for describing the whole control system or comparing hot and cold responses.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (Biology only)
core.p: AQA 8461 (Biology only, Homeostasis and response) expects you to explain how the body **monitors and controls its internal temperature**. You must know that the **thermoregulatory centre in the brain** contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood, that **temperature receptors in the skin** also send impulses to this centre, and that the centre then triggers **effectors** to bring temperature back to normal. You must be able to describe the responses to being **too hot** (sweating, vasodilation) and **too cold** (shivering, vasoconstriction, hairs standing on end, no sweating) and explain **why** each response works. This is a classic **negative feedback** example, so examiners also like to test the control loop itself.

bullets: **Optimum temperature** for most human enzymes is about **37 °C**, so the body is held at this value.
**Too high**: enzymes are **denatured** (the shape of the active site changes permanently), so reactions stop working properly.
**Too low**: molecules move more slowly, there are **fewer collisions** and **less energy**, so reaction rates fall.
Because body reactions release energy (respiration), humans are **warm-blooded**: they can keep a steady temperature independent of surroundings.
Control involves **automatic** systems: you do not have to think about sweating or shivering.
Other conditions controlled by homeostasis include **blood glucose concentration** and **water content** (separate spec points).
Remember: homeostasis keeps conditions **within a narrow range**, not at one fixed value all the time.
core.h: Why body temperature must be controlled: homeostasis and enzymes
core.p: **Homeostasis** is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes. Body temperature is one of these conditions. Almost every chemical reaction in the body is controlled by an **enzyme**, and enzymes have an **optimum temperature**: if the temperature rises too far the shape of the active site changes and the enzyme is **denatured**, so it can no longer catalyse its reaction; if the temperature falls too far the reactions simply become **too slow** to keep the cell alive. The human body therefore keeps its core temperature close to **37 °C**, even when the surroundings are very hot or very cold.

bullets: **Receptors**: skin temperature receptors and the blood-temperature receptors inside the thermoregulatory centre.
**Information travels** from skin receptors along **sensory neurones** to the brain as **electrical impulses**.
**Coordination centre**: the **thermoregulatory centre** in the brain (part of the **hypothalamus**, an extra term you may meet).
The centre sends **nervous impulses** to the effectors to bring about the response.
**Effectors** include **sweat glands** (glands release sweat) and **muscles** (which contract).
The whole loop is automatic and fast, so a change of even a fraction of a degree is corrected.
Use the general pathway in answers: **stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response**.
core.h: The control system: receptors, coordination centre and effectors
core.p: All automatic control systems in the body have the same three parts: **receptors** that detect a **stimulus** (a change), a **coordination centre** that receives and processes the information and decides on a response, and **effectors** that carry out the response. In temperature control the **receptors** are the **temperature-sensitive cells in the thermoregulatory centre** (which detect blood temperature) and the **receptors in the skin** (which detect surface temperature). The **coordination centre** is the **thermoregulatory centre in the brain**. The **effectors** are the **sweat glands**, the **muscles** (skeletal muscles and the small muscles in the walls of blood vessels and attached to hairs).

bullets: **Negative feedback** = a change is detected and the response **opposes** that change, returning conditions towards normal.
The loop is continuous: the temperature **rises slightly, response cools it, falls slightly, response warms it**, and so on.
On a graph of body temperature against time, the line **fluctuates a little above and below 37 °C** rather than being perfectly flat.
If the response did not switch off at the right time, the body would **overshoot** and swing too far the other way.
The **thermoregulatory centre** is like a thermostat: it compares the current temperature with the set point.

Think of a **central heating thermostat**: it switches the boiler on when it is too cold and off when warm enough (a good model, but it breaks down because the body uses many different effectors at once).
Negative feedback also controls blood glucose (insulin and glucagon) and water balance, so recognising the pattern helps across the whole topic.
core.h: Negative feedback: how the loop corrects itself
core.p: Body temperature control is an example of **negative feedback**: whenever the temperature moves **away** from the normal value, the response **reverses the change** and brings it back. If the body gets **too hot**, the responses (sweating, vasodilation) cool it down; if it gets **too cold**, the responses (shivering, vasoconstriction) warm it up. Once the temperature returns to 37 °C the receptors stop sending signals and the responses switch off, which prevents the temperature overshooting. Because the responses are driven by the change they correct, the temperature **oscillates in a small range** around the set point rather than staying exactly constant.

bullets: **Sweat glands release more sweat** onto the surface of the skin.
**Blood vessels dilate** (get wider) so more blood flows through the capillaries near the skin surface.
Both responses **increase energy transfer from the body to the environment**.
Hairs lie **flat** against the skin so less air is trapped, allowing energy to escape more easily.
Muscles are relaxed, so there is no extra energy released by shivering.
Behavioural responses also help (taking off clothes, moving into shade, drinking) but these are not part of the automatic control system.
If the temperature is not brought down, enzymes could start to denature, which is dangerous.
core.h: When the body is too hot: overview of the responses
core.p: When the blood and skin become too warm, the thermoregulatory centre triggers responses that **increase the transfer of energy from the body to the surroundings**. The two responses you must know are **sweating** (sweat glands release sweat onto the skin) and **vasodilation** (the blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries widen). Together they increase the rate at which thermal energy leaves the body, and the temperature returns to 37 °C. At the same time, the muscles do not shiver and the hairs lie flat.

bullets: **Sweat** is a mixture of water, salts and small amounts of waste (urea).
Cooling happens because **evaporation of sweat transfers energy from the skin** to the surroundings (the sweat gains the energy it needs to evaporate).
Sweat that **drips off** or is wiped away does **not** cool you effectively; the cooling needs **evaporation**.
In **humid** air, sweat evaporates slowly, so cooling is less effective and you feel hotter.
In **dry, windy** air sweat evaporates quickly, so cooling is more effective.
Heavy sweating loses **water and ions**, so you must replace them (link to water balance).
Do not say that sweat 'cools the body down' on its own: you must say the **evaporation** transfers energy from the skin.
core.p: When the body is too hot, **sweat glands release sweat**, which is mostly water with small amounts of salt. The sweat spreads over the skin surface, and the water in it then **evaporates**. For a liquid to turn into a gas the particles need energy, and this energy is **taken from the skin and the body** as the water evaporates, so the body is **cooled**. The more sweat evaporates, the greater the cooling effect. This is why you feel cool when you get out of a swimming pool: the water on your skin evaporates and takes thermal energy with it.

bullets: **Vasodilation** = blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries **dilate**, so **more blood flows near the surface**.
The energy is **transferred from the blood to the environment** (mostly by **radiation**), cooling the blood.
The cooler blood then returns to the body core, helping lower the whole body temperature.
Vasodilation is carried out by the **muscle in the walls** of the blood vessels, which relaxes.
**Important**: the blood vessels do **not** move closer to the skin surface or change position; only their **diameter** changes.
This is the origin of the red face seen after hard exercise or on a hot day.
Mark scheme phrase: **'more blood flows through capillaries near the surface of the skin, so more energy is transferred to the surroundings'**.
core.h: Vasodilation: how wider blood vessels lose heat
core.p: **Vasodilation** is the widening of the **blood vessels that supply the skin capillaries**. The walls of these vessels contain muscle which **relaxes**, so the vessels become wider and **more blood flows near the surface of the skin**. The blood is warm from the body's core, so more energy is transferred from the blood to the surroundings, mainly by **radiation** (and some conduction and convection). The skin looks **red** or flushed when you are hot because of the extra blood near the surface.

bullets: **Skeletal muscles contract rapidly** (shiver), which **releases energy** by respiration.
**Blood vessels constrict** (get narrower) so **less blood flows near the skin surface**, reducing energy loss.
**Hairs stand on end** (hair erector muscles contract), trapping a layer of **insulating air** next to the skin.
**Sweating stops**, so no energy is lost by evaporation.
Together the responses **increase energy production** and **reduce energy loss**.
The skin looks **pale** when you are cold because less blood reaches the surface.
These responses are all automatic and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre.
core.h: When the body is too cold: overview of the responses
core.p: When the body is too cold, the thermoregulatory centre triggers responses that **reduce energy loss** and **increase energy release**. The responses you must know are **shivering** (skeletal muscles contract rapidly), **vasoconstriction** (blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries narrow), **hairs standing on end** and **sweating stops**. These help bring the temperature back up to 37 °C.

bullets: Shivering = **skeletal muscles contract** quickly and repeatedly without movement.
**Respiration** in muscle cells releases energy; some of it is **transferred as thermal energy** to the body.
The warmed blood is carried by the **circulatory system** to the rest of the body.
Shivering needs **more glucose and oxygen**, so breathing and heart rate can increase.
The effect is limited: if shivering cannot keep up with heat loss, body temperature will keep falling.
Do not say that shivering 'creates heat from nothing': it **transfers energy from respiration**.
Shivering is the opposite of the sweating response: **sweating cools, shivering warms**.
core.p: **Shivering** is the rapid, involuntary contraction and relaxation of the skeletal muscles. Muscle contraction needs energy, and this is supplied by **respiration**, which is an **exothermic** reaction: it also transfers thermal energy to the body. The extra energy released from the muscle cells warms the blood passing through them, and this warm blood circulates round the body and raises the temperature. Shivering uses a lot of energy from glucose, which is why you feel tired and hungry after being very cold.

bullets: **Vasoconstriction** = blood vessels supplying skin capillaries **constrict**, so **less blood flows near the skin surface**.
This **reduces the energy transferred** to the surroundings and keeps the core warm.
**Erect hairs** trap a layer of **air**, which acts as an **insulating layer** (air is a poor conductor of heat).
In furry animals this response is very effective; in humans it gives goose bumps and has little effect.
**No sweat** is produced, so no energy is lost by evaporation.
Again: vessels do **not** move; only the **width of the vessel** changes.
Skin goes pale and hands and feet feel cold because less warm blood reaches them.
core.h: Vasoconstriction, erect hairs and no sweating
core.p: **Vasoconstriction** is the narrowing of the blood vessels that supply the skin capillaries. The muscle in their walls **contracts**, so the vessels get narrower and **less blood flows near the surface** of the skin. Less energy is transferred from the blood to the surroundings, so more energy is kept in the body core. At the same time the **hair erector muscles contract and the hairs stand on end**, trapping a layer of air which is a good **insulator** because air is a poor conductor; in humans this has only a small effect because we have so little body hair, but you feel it as goose bumps. **Sweating stops** because evaporation would remove energy.

bullets: **Sweat glands**: sweat when hot → evaporation cools; no sweat when cold → no cooling.
**Skin blood vessels**: **dilate** when hot → more blood near surface; **constrict** when cold → less blood near surface.
**Skeletal muscles**: relaxed when hot; **shiver** when cold, releasing energy from respiration.
**Hairs**: lie flat when hot; stand on end when cold to trap insulating air.
Hot responses **increase** energy transfer to surroundings; cold responses **decrease** it and **increase** energy release.
Use the words **'dilate'** and **'constrict'** for blood vessels (not 'widen the skin' or 'move to the surface').
In a table question, check each row is correct for the right condition (hot or cold).
core.h: Comparing the responses: hot and cold side by side
core.p: Putting the two sets of responses side by side helps you remember them and answer comparison questions. For each effector, the hot response and the cold response are exact opposites. The sweat glands release sweat when hot and release none when cold; the blood vessels dilate when hot and constrict when cold; the skeletal muscles relax when hot and shiver when cold; the hairs lie flat when hot and stand up when cold.

bullets: **Overheating**: sweat loses **water and ions**; dehydration reduces the ability to sweat; enzymes can be **denatured** at high temperatures.
**Overcooling (hypothermia)**: energy lost faster than it can be replaced, so reactions slow down.
Small animals and babies have a **large SA:V**, so they lose energy quickly and need to eat more or be kept warm.
Large animals with a **small SA:V** (e.g. elephants) lose less energy, so they need large ears and other features to lose heat.
Heavy exercise **increases energy release** (respiration), so the body needs to lose extra heat by sweating and vasodilation.
Behaviour such as **clothing, shelter and drinking water** helps the automatic system.
Illness such as **fever** raises the set point, which is why you can feel cold and shiver when your temperature is high.
core.h: What goes wrong: extreme temperatures and the limits of control
core.p: The control system works well within limits but can be overwhelmed. If the surroundings are very hot or the person exercises hard without enough water, sweating cannot keep up and the **body temperature rises**; if it rises too high, enzymes begin to **denature** and the person can become seriously ill. In very cold conditions, shivering and vasoconstriction cannot replace the energy being lost, so the body temperature falls; low temperatures slow the enzyme-controlled reactions, and the person can become seriously ill. Babies and elderly people are at greater risk because their control is less effective, and small bodies lose energy faster because they have a **larger surface area to volume ratio**.

bullets: **Enzymes (4.2)**: optimum temperature and denaturing explain why temperature must be controlled.
**Respiration (4.4)**: exothermic reaction; more respiration in muscles gives more heat.
**Nervous system (4.5.1)**: impulses carried by neurones; the thermoregulatory centre is in the brain.
**Circulatory system (4.2)**: blood carries energy to and from the skin.
**Physics link**: energy transfer by conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation.
**Maths skill**: read a graph of body temperature against time and describe the fluctuation around 37 °C; calculate rates of change.
**Command words**: 'Explain' needs a reason (e.g. because evaporation takes energy from the skin); 'Describe' needs the sequence of events.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: This topic links to many others. **Enzymes** explain why 37 °C matters; **respiration** explains where the energy for shivering comes from; the **nervous system** explains how information reaches the brain and how the effectors are triggered; and the **circulatory system** explains how blood carries thermal energy around the body. **Homeostasis** of blood glucose and water follows the same negative feedback pattern, so use the same structure (receptor, coordinator, effector) in every answer.

exam: **State (1 mark)**: 'the thermoregulatory centre in the brain' for where temperature is monitored; 'sweat glands', 'blood vessels' or 'skeletal muscles' for effectors.

**Describe the response when too hot (2-3 marks)**: sweat glands release sweat; sweat evaporates, transferring energy from the skin; blood vessels dilate so more blood flows near the skin surface and more energy is transferred to the surroundings.

**Describe the response when too cold (3-4 marks)**: skeletal muscles contract (shiver) so respiration releases energy; blood vessels constrict so less blood flows near the surface; hairs stand on end to trap insulating air; sweating stops.
**Explain why shivering warms you**: muscles contract, which needs energy from respiration, and respiration transfers energy to the body, warming the blood.
**Explain evaporation**: say the sweat **evaporates** and **takes energy from the skin**; avoid 'sweat cools you down' without a reason.

**Describe the control system (4-6 marks)**: receptors in the skin and blood detect temperature, impulses go to the thermoregulatory centre, which sends impulses to effectors (muscles and glands) and the response returns temperature to 37 °C (negative feedback).
**Why 37 °C?** Enzymes work best (optimum) at this temperature; too high and they are denatured, too low and reactions are too slow.
**Graphs of body temperature**: describe the fluctuation about 37 °C, quote values with units, and link rises to cooling responses and falls to warming responses.
**Table questions**: check each row is correct for hot or cold; use 'dilate' and 'constrict' for vessels.
**Command words**: 'Describe' = sequence of events; 'Explain' = reasons with 'because' or 'so'; 'Suggest' = apply your knowledge to a new situation (such as a runner or an arctic animal).
**Maths**: rate of change = change in temperature ÷ time; give units such as °C per minute.

mistakes.r: Blood vessels do not move; the vessels supplying the skin capillaries dilate, so more blood flows near the surface.
mistakes.w: Blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when you are hot.

mistakes.r: Sweat cools the body because its evaporation transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings.
mistakes.w: Sweating cools you because sweat is cold.

mistakes.r: Shivering is rapid muscle contraction; respiration in the muscles releases energy that warms the body.
Hairs lie flat when hot so less air is trapped; they stand on end when cold to trap an insulating layer of air.
mistakes.w: When hot, the hairs lie flat to keep you warm.

mistakes.r: Vasoconstriction is the narrowing (constriction) of blood vessels; vasodilation is the widening.
mistakes.w: Vasoconstriction means blood vessels get wider.

mistakes.r: The thermoregulatory centre is in the brain; the skin contains receptors that send impulses to it.
mistakes.w: The thermoregulatory centre is in the skin.

mistakes.r: Negative feedback keeps it fluctuating within a narrow range around 37 °C.
mistakes.w: Body temperature stays at exactly 37 °C all the time.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured when the active site changes shape.
mistakes.w: Enzymes die when it is too hot.

mistakes.r: Sweating is a response to being too hot and cools you by evaporation.
mistakes.w: Sweating heats you up because your body is working.

summary: AQA Biology-only 4.5.2: you must explain how body temperature is monitored by the thermoregulatory centre (blood temperature receptors) and skin receptors, and how the body responds when too hot (sweating, vasodilation) and too cold (shivering, vasoconstriction, hairs on end, no sweating) as an example of negative feedback. It matters because enzymes only work properly near 37 °C and this topic is full of explain-why questions.

terms.d: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function in response to internal and external changes.
The part of the brain that monitors and controls body temperature; it contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood.
A control system in which a change is detected and the response reverses the change, returning conditions to normal.
A cell that detects a stimulus, such as a change in temperature.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response to a stimulus.
The part of the nervous system (such as the brain) that receives information from receptors and decides on the response.
A change in the environment or in the body that is detected by a receptor.
A liquid, mostly water, released by sweat glands onto the skin; its evaporation transfers energy from the skin.
The change of a liquid to a gas at a temperature below its boiling point, which takes energy from the surroundings.
The widening of the blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries, so more blood flows near the skin surface and more energy is transferred to the surroundings.
The narrowing of the blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries, so less blood flows near the skin surface and less energy is transferred to the surroundings.
The rapid contraction of skeletal muscles, which releases energy by respiration to warm the body.
Muscle attached to bones that contracts to cause movement; it shivers when the body is too cold.
The smallest blood vessels, with thin walls, through which substances and energy are exchanged.
A biological catalyst that speeds up reactions; most human enzymes work best at about 37 °C.
Describes an enzyme whose active site has changed shape, usually at high temperature, so it can no longer catalyse its reaction.
The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
The normal value that a control system tries to maintain, e.g. 37 °C for body temperature.
A layer, such as trapped air or fat, that reduces the transfer of energy to the surroundings.

worked.ans: Receptors detect the rise in temperature and the thermoregulatory centre sends impulses to effectors. Sweat glands release sweat which evaporates, taking energy from the skin. The blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries dilate (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface and more energy is transferred to the surroundings. This cools the body back to 37 °C.
worked.q: Explain how the body responds when its temperature rises above 37 °C on a hot day. (4 marks)
steps: Receptors in the skin and in the thermoregulatory centre detect the rise in temperature.
The thermoregulatory centre sends impulses to the effectors.
Sweat glands release sweat, and the evaporation of sweat transfers energy from the skin to the surroundings.
Blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries dilate, so more blood flows near the surface and more energy is transferred to the surroundings, bringing the temperature back to 37 °C.

worked.ans: 0.07 °C per minute. The temperature rises because muscles respire faster during exercise, releasing more energy, some of which is transferred as heat to the body faster than it is lost.
worked.q: A hiker's body temperature rises from 37.0 °C to 38.4 °C during 20 minutes of hard exercise. Calculate the mean rate of temperature rise and explain why the body temperature rises during exercise. (3 marks)
steps: Exercise needs more energy, so respiration in muscles increases, releasing more thermal energy than is lost.

worked.ans: Receptors in the skin and brain detect the fall in temperature and the thermoregulatory centre sends impulses to effectors. The skeletal muscles shiver, so respiration releases energy that warms the blood. The blood vessels supplying the skin constrict (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface and less energy is transferred to the surroundings. Hairs stand on end to trap an insulating layer of air, and sweating stops so energy is not lost by evaporation. These responses bring the temperature back to 37 °C, the optimum for enzymes, and are an example of negative feedback.
worked.q: Describe and explain the responses of a person who has walked out into freezing weather. (6 marks)
steps: Receptors in the skin and thermoregulatory centre detect a fall in temperature.
The thermoregulatory centre sends impulses to effectors.
Skeletal muscles contract rapidly (shiver); respiration releases energy to warm the body.
Blood vessels supplying the skin capillaries constrict, so less blood flows near the surface and less energy is lost.
Hairs stand on end, trapping an insulating layer of air; sweating stops so no energy is lost by evaporation.
The temperature returns to 37 °C, which keeps enzymes working at their optimum (negative feedback).
